A path must visit every vertex exactly once
One direction has cyclic or modular adjacency
Endpoints or endpoint layers are prescribed

steps.detail: Translate allowed consecutive positions into graph edges and identify periodic directions.
Track how a cut through the narrow direction can be connected by the partial path.
Use degree, parity, and endpoint constraints to retain only one-component Hamiltonian paths.

name: Self-Composed Superadditive Function Inequalities
description: Analyzes integer-valued functions whose values at sums are bounded through a self-composition term, combining iterative inequalities with constructions for attainable values.
applicability: A function on positive integers is constrained for every pair of inputs
The inequality contains both f(a+b) and f(f(b))
The goal asks for possible values of f at a fixed input

steps.detail: Use small or repeated inputs to obtain monotonicity and growth constraints.
Compare repeated applications of the inequality without assuming equality.
Prove necessary value bounds, then verify generic function families attain admissible cases.

name: Mutual Polynomial Root-Multiplicity Encoding
description: Uses factorization identities to convert sequences of integer exponents into reciprocal constraints on root locations and multiplicities.
applicability: Two polynomial products are equal for all x
Exponents or multiplicities are indexed by integers
A second identity swaps the roles of the exponent sequences

steps.detail: Equate each root multiplicity on both sides of each identity.
View multiplicity data as maps on the finite index set and apply the reciprocal relation.
Classify allowed cycles or fixed points before summing any weighted quantity.

name: Local 2x2 Tiling Constraints to Global Row-Column States
description: Derives global structure from a condition imposed on every 2x2 window of a board, using row/column states and compatible transitions.
applicability: Tiles occupy a rectangular board
Every 2x2 sub-board satisfies a coverage or vacancy condition
The task asks for a count or extremal placement

steps.detail: Represent each row boundary or window by a finite state.
Translate the 2x2 condition into compatibility rules between adjacent states.
Use extremal tile count to force the remaining state pattern or enumerate transitions.

name: Polyomino Covering via Coloring Invariants and Constructions
description: Establishes lower bounds and constructions for polyomino coverings by combining residue colorings with recursive or strip-based decompositions.
applicability: A board subset must be tiled or covered by fixed polyominoes
Only selected colors or cells are required
The task asks whether a cover exists or minimizes tile count

steps.detail: Select a periodic coloring whose tile color signatures constrain any cover.
Compare required color counts with each tile's possible contribution.
Give a repeating strip, block, or inductive construction attaining the bound.

name: Planar Red-Blue Separation by Line Arrangements
description: Bounds the number of lines needed to separate two finite point sets in general position, using arrangement complexity and extremal configurations.
applicability: Red and blue points are in the plane with no three collinear
Lines may not pass through marked points
Every final region must be monochromatic
A worst-case minimum number of lines is sought

steps.detail: Use alternating or convex-position configurations for lower bounds.
Add lines through gaps or supporting directions to isolate colors progressively.
Check that the final arrangement cannot leave a mixed-color region.

name: Adversarial Piece Placement through Packing and Hitting Sets
description: Obtains guaranteed placement counts in alternating placement games by pairing a packing lower bound with an opponent's blocking or hitting-set upper bound.
applicability: Players alternately place pieces under attack or occupancy restrictions
One player seeks a guaranteed number of placements
The board is rectangular and piece attacks are local or geometric

steps.detail: Partition the board into blocks or choose a sparse set that preserves legal placements.
Show each opponent move can destroy only boundedly many protected choices.
Use a blocking arrangement or counting cover for the opposing bound.

name: Difference Bases for Recurrence-Generated Target Sets
description: Constructs and lower-bounds integer sets whose pairwise differences contain a prescribed recurrence sequence, using telescoping identities and graph representations.
applicability: A set must realize many specified integers as differences
Targets obey a linear recurrence
The objective is to minimize the size of the realizing set

steps.detail: Use recurrence relations to express targets as differences of a compact auxiliary sequence.
List vertices whose pairwise differences cover all required targets.
Model required differences as edges and use degree, path, or counting constraints.

name: Max-Plus Integer Vector Generation and Dimension Bounds
description: Analyzes the closure of integer vectors under componentwise maximum and addition, separating coordinatewise invariants from explicit generating families.
applicability: Vectors are combined by ordinary addition and componentwise maximum
The goal is the minimum number of generators for all integer vectors
Dimension or coordinate independence is central

steps.detail: Track translation, coordinate differences, and tropical convexity invariants.
Show too few generators cannot independently control every coordinate pattern.
Construct a small generic family and prove it produces the target closure.

name: Dense Graph Complete-Bipartite Homomorphism Lower Bounds
description: Lower-bounds ordered complete bipartite configurations in a dense graph by averaging common-neighborhood sizes and applying convexity.
applicability: A graph has an edge-density lower bound
Ordered vertices may repeat
Every cross-pair between two tuples must be an edge
A minimum count of complete bipartite patterns is requested

steps.detail: Sum powers of common-neighborhood sizes over one side of the tuple.
Use edge density to lower-bound the relevant average neighborhood size.
Use Jensen or power-mean on the nonnegative counts and track ordered repetitions.

name: Divisibility-Preserving Integer Function Classification
description: Classifies functions constrained by divisibility of output differences against polynomial input differences, using small differences, valuations, and completeness checks.
applicability: A function on integers has a divisibility condition for every distinct pair
The divisor involves f(a)-f(b)
The target asks to count functions or characterize exceptional exponents

steps.detail: Use small input differences to constrain local output gaps.
Compare valuations of polynomial differences across carefully chosen pairs.
Prove both that each candidate family works and that no other family exists.

name: GCD-Intersection Graphs in Short Integer Intervals
description: Treats pairwise non-coprimality constraints as graph conditions on integers in a short interval, combining prime-divisibility classes with extremal constructions.
applicability: A set of integers lies in a bounded interval
Every selected triple must contain a pair with gcd greater than one
The goal is a maximum cardinality

steps.detail: Represent forbidden all-coprime triples as independent triples in a graph complement.
Use divisibility by small primes to construct large admissible families.
Control isolated or mutually coprime elements using interval and residue arguments.

name: Compactness in Euclidean Spaces via Heine-Borel
description: Selects and proves equivalent compactness characterizations for subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
applicability: The setting is a subset of R^n
The question asks which compactness characterization is correct
Options mention closedness, boundedness, or open covers

steps.detail: Confirm the statement is in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
Use compact iff closed and bounded, and compact iff every open cover has a finite subcover.
Provide an unbounded closed or bounded open counterexample as appropriate.

name: Elliptic Dirichlet PDE Discretization Selection
description: Chooses standard numerical discretizations for elliptic boundary-value problems with prescribed Dirichlet data.
applicability: The equation is Laplace or Poisson type on a domain
Boundary values are prescribed
The task asks for a standard discretization method

steps.detail: Recognize an elliptic boundary-value problem.
Use finite differences on structured grids or finite elements on general domains.
Incorporate the Dirichlet values into the discrete system.

name: Seasonal Adjustment Method Identification
description: Identifies standard methods for removing seasonal effects from a time series and distinguishes smoothing from decomposition approaches.
applicability: A time-series question asks for common seasonal adjustment methods
The expected response is a named method rather than a derivation

steps.detail: Separate periodic effects from trend and irregular variation.
Use moving averages and seasonal decomposition as baseline methods.

name: Nonlinear Regression Parameter Estimation Basics
description: Identifies least-squares fitting as the standard baseline for estimating nonlinear regression parameters, with numerical optimization used to solve the objective.
applicability: A regression model is nonlinear in its parameters
The question asks for the usual parameter-estimation method
Options mix an objective with numerical solvers

steps.detail: Distinguish least squares or likelihood criteria from iterative algorithms.
For ordinary nonlinear regression, state nonlinear least squares unless a probabilistic likelihood model is specified.

name: Nested-Index Integer Sequence: Exhaustive Branch Classification
description: For a nonnegative-integer sequence satisfying an identity of the form f(f(f(p))) = f(p+1) + 1, classify all branches of the iterated value map instead of guessing one affine sequence. Use collision propagation, gap states, and explicit existence checks so that no exceptional branch is discarded.
applicability: A sequence of nonnegative integers has nested subscripts such as a_{a_{a_p}} for every p
The relation combines repeated value-map iteration with an ordinary index shift p to p+1
The question asks for all possible values of a distant term
A simple affine candidate can be verified but does not by itself prove uniqueness

steps.detail: Set f(n)=a_n and preserve the condition as f^3(p)=f(p+1)+1. Never simplify f^3(p) to a linear expression or assume f(n)=n+c before a classification proof.

From f(r)=f(s), substitute r and s into the defining identity to obtain f(r+1)=f(s+1), then iterate. Analyze a first collision or least image value; reject every collision pattern that forces an incompatible bounded or periodic tail.

Use the collision analysis to justify the permitted order among f(n), f(n+1), f^2(n), and n+1. Only then introduce d_n=f(n)-n and derive the finite allowed transitions for these gaps from f^3(p)=f(p+1)+1.

The gap-state analysis contains an ordinary successor branch and one exceptional forced-orbit branch. Trace each branch from its initial state until its stable regime; eliminate every other state with a concrete contradiction to the equation or nonnegativity.

steps.step: Evaluate the target only after classification
steps.detail: For a requested index N, the two surviving branches give the symbolic target forms N+1 and N+5. Substitute N only in the final response and list both values, because a request for all possibilities is not satisfied by one constructed branch.
Substitute each surviving branch back into f^3(p)=f(p+1)+1 for arbitrary p. Then state which collision and gap cases were ruled out; checking the ordinary branch alone is not a uniqueness proof.

example.problem: Let b: Z_{>=0} -> Z_{>=0} satisfy b(b(b(q)))=b(q+2)+2 for every q>=0. Classify the possible values of b(M) for a specified large index M.
example.solution: Preserve the nested iteration exactly, use equality propagation to constrain collisions, and derive state transitions for the allowed index gaps. Separate every viable initial-state branch, verify each candidate structure for all q, and only then evaluate the requested index. Do not infer uniqueness from a single affine construction.

name: Alternating Domino Placement on a Path via Minimax Segment States
description: Solves a two-player perfect-information game on a one-dimensional row of consecutive squares, where each move places a domino on two adjacent currently uncovered squares and splits an uncovered interval into smaller intervals. One player maximizes the final number of uncovered squares, while the other minimizes it. Model legal placements as edges of a path graph, preserve the alternating move order, and analyze the resulting multiset of disjoint uncovered segments by minimax rather than treating the task as a static domino tiling problem.
applicability: The board is a single row or path of consecutive cells or vertices.
Each legal move selects two adjacent unoccupied cells and no overlap is allowed.
Play ends when every remaining uncovered segment has length zero or one.
The players have opposite objectives concerning the number of moves, covered cells, or uncovered cells.
A move in an interval of length L removes two adjacent cells and creates left and right residual intervals whose lengths sum to L-2.
The requested result is a guaranteed outcome under optimal play, not merely the maximum matching size of the original path.

steps.step: Convert the terminal objective into a move-count objective
steps.detail: If the board has N cells and the game uses M dominoes, then the terminal number of uncovered cells is N-2M. State explicitly which player minimizes M and which player maximizes M; do not confuse this with maximizing the number of cells covered on a single move.

steps.step: Represent every position by uncovered intervals
steps.detail: After any sequence of moves, delete covered cells and record the lengths of all maximal uncovered consecutive segments as a sorted multiset S. A segment of length 0 or 1 has no legal move. A move in a segment of length L>=2 at offset r creates two segments of lengths r and L-2-r, together with all untouched segments.

steps.step: Write the exact alternating minimax recurrence
steps.detail: Sort the positive segment lengths in S. If a move chooses length L in S and leaves r and L-2-r cells (0<=r<=L-2), define T(S,L,r)=sort((S\{L}) union {r,L-2-r} with zero lengths removed). Let A(S) be the minimum possible number of remaining dominoes when the player minimizing M moves, and B(S) the maximum when the player maximizing M moves. For every nonterminal S, A(S)=min_{L in S,L>=2;0<=r<=L-2}[1+B(T(S,L,r))] and B(S)=max_{L in S,L>=2;0<=r<=L-2}[1+A(T(S,L,r))]. Set A(S)=B(S)=0 only when every length is at most 1. Since the player maximizing uncovered cells U=N-2M minimizes M, use A for that player's turns and B for the opponent's turns.

steps.step: Reject invalid scalar and additive reductions
steps.detail: Never replace the multiset state by a recurrence in one scalar length after a split: the two residual segments share one global alternating turn sequence. In particular, do not write A(L) from sums such as B(r)+B(L-2-r), and do not assign each component an independent next turn. Any conjectured formula must first agree with the exact A/B recurrence on canonical multi-segment states such as (1,4), (2,3), and their legal moves.

steps.step: Build an exact boundary table before guessing a formula
steps.detail: For a bounded total length b, compute both A(S) and B(S) bottom-up for every sorted multiset S with sum(S)<=b, processing smaller total length first. Record the full transition witness: for A, a minimizing pair (L,r); for B, a maximizing pair (L,r). A claimed value for a one-interval state (L) is admissible only if its witness transition is checked against the already computed multi-interval state T((L),L,r). Use this table to reject a parity-only or maximum-matching claim as soon as one descendant multiset contradicts it.

steps.step: State block bounds as response invariants
steps.detail: For a candidate block size q, define explicit turn-labelled boundary families F_A(k,s) and F_B(k,s), where k is the number of complete blocks and s is a bounded residual multiset. Prove an upper bound by: for every opponent move T(S,L,r), exhibit one legal response and show 1+1 plus the remaining play reaches the required earlier family. Prove the lower bound separately by showing that every legal minimizing move enters a family whose certified lower value applies. Keep the move count in each transition: if a two-move exchange removes a block, the recurrence must have the form value(k,s)=2+value(k-1,s'), not an uncounted state equivalence.

Compute the recurrence exactly for a sufficiently broad range of short interval multisets. Then prove any observed simplification: reflection symmetry r and L-2-r give the same state; zero segments may be discarded; equal segment lengths can be grouped; and any proposed periodic or block recurrence must be verified by showing that every legal split maps to one of the proved state classes.

steps.step: Build a finite boundary-state or block induction
steps.detail: Partition a long path into repeated blocks plus a bounded boundary remainder. Define a small list of boundary states describing which cells near a block boundary remain available and whose turn it is. Prove an induction transition for each player: the minimizing player supplies a response that keeps the state in the claimed lower-move class, while the maximizing player supplies a response that realizes the claimed upper-move class. For every response, count the initiating move and prove that the full residual multiset, not merely one component, enters an earlier covered class. A diagram or ordered tuple of all remaining segment lengths must accompany each claimed block transition.

For the minimizing player, give an explicit response strategy after every possible opponent move and show it limits the total number of future dominoes. For the maximizing player, give an explicit forcing strategy or invariant showing that fewer dominoes cannot suffice. Do not accept a construction for one player as proof of the game value without the opponent bound.

Express N by the proved block length plus a remainder. Analyze each allowable remainder with the same minimax recurrence, combine it with the block induction, obtain the optimal domino count M, and only then convert back to N-2M uncovered cells. Check that the final result has the same parity as N.

example.problem: A finite collection of disjoint intervals is represented by their positive integer lengths. Two agents alternately select one interval of length at least two and replace it by two residual intervals whose lengths sum to two less than the selected length. One agent seeks to minimize the total number of selections, while the other seeks to maximize it. Determine the optimal terminal selection count from an initial single interval of symbolic length R.
example.solution: Canonicalize the entire multiset of interval lengths and define one minimization and one maximization value with the current player included. Enumerate all legal replacements for small boundary states, including states with more than one interval; do not add independent values of the two residual intervals. Then seek a block invariant stable under every possible split. Prove upper and lower bounds separately using legal response moves, and verify the claimed recurrence against every residue and terminal state before applying it to the symbolic initial length.

name: Dense-Graph Homomorphism Counting with Density Normalization
description: Counts ordered tuples with repeated vertices allowed in a simple undirected graph when every vertex in one group is adjacent to every vertex in another. Preserve the distinction between |E|/N^2, ordered edge density, and |E|/binom(N,2), and keep the handshake factor explicit.
applicability: The graph is simple and undirected with |E| >= rho N^2.
The target is a K_{s,t}-type ordered homomorphism count with repeated entries allowed.
The proof uses common-neighborhood sizes, degree moments, Jensen, or Holder inequalities.

steps.detail: Define the ordered tuple count H and record sum_v d(v)=2|E| before applying any inequality.
Set c(y_1,...,y_t)=|intersection N(y_j)| and write H=sum c(y)^s.
Use Jensen or Holder only after computing sum_y c(y)=sum_v d(v)^t; keep rho symbolic until the final substitution.
Set s=t=1 and verify that H counts ordered edges, exposing any missing or extra factor of two.
Verify a graph construction satisfies the finite edge constraint and attains the derived bound.

example.problem: A simple undirected graph on N vertices has at least rho N^2 edges. Count ordered (u+v)-tuples with repetitions allowed such that every first-group vertex is adjacent to every second-group vertex.
example.solution: Use common-neighborhood power sums, the handshake identity, convexity, a smallest-parameter normalization check, and an independent extremal construction.

name: Right-Triangle Segment Ratios by Sine-Law and Coordinate Verification
description: Solves ratios determined by rays meeting a side of a right triangle. The safeguards are correct ray orientation, explicit angle sums, independent segment formulas, and a second coordinate or trigonometric check.
applicability: A right triangle is specified by its hypotenuse and an acute angle.
Points lie on a common side and rays from a vertex have prescribed angles.
The target is a scaled ratio of two subsegments.

steps.detail: Identify the right angle and draw each ray on the side consistent with the stated point.
Apply the sine rule in its auxiliary triangle and derive every angle from the original triangle.
Apply the sine rule independently; do not infer it from symmetry.
Relate the original sides by sine or cosine and simplify only after checking supplementary angles.
Place one side on a coordinate axis and intersect both rays with the side line.

example.problem: In a right triangle, two rays with symbolic angle offsets meet the opposite leg at two points. Determine a scaled ratio of the resulting subsegments.
example.solution: Determine all angles, derive both lengths by the sine rule, eliminate the common scale, and verify the result by coordinates.

name: Divisibility-Constrained Integer Function Classification
description: Classifies functions on all integers satisfying a universal divisibility relation between function differences and power differences, then determines a parity property of the number of functions.
applicability: The condition holds for every distinct integer pair and a normalization such as g(1)=1 is given.
The exponent is split into odd and 2-adic parts.
The problem asks for all function families or parity-indexed exponents.

steps.detail: Use pairs involving 0, 1, -1, and consecutive integers to constrain constants, signs, and translations.
Establish necessity and substitute every candidate family back into the universal divisibility condition.
Write n=2^e m with m odd and treat e=0 and e>0 separately; do not transfer odd-case counts to even n.
Factor the complete function count and apply the divisor-count square criterion only after the count is proved.
Test odd square, odd nonsquare, even, and higher 2-adic examples and verify no branch is omitted.

example.problem: Let h:Z->Z satisfy h(1)=1 and h(r)-h(s) divide r^q-s^q for all distinct r,s. Classify all admissible h and determine which positive q have a function count equal to twice an odd number.
example.solution: Extract forced values, prove candidate families in both directions, split q by its 2-adic valuation, factor the count, and verify representative branches before indexing.

name: All-Position Digit-Deletion Recursion and Maximal-State Search
description: Finds the largest recursively valid integer when deleting one digit must produce a divisor that is valid again. Deletion can occur at any position, so prefix-only extension and greedy search are incomplete.
applicability: Digits are pairwise distinct and any one digit may be deleted.
The resulting integer must divide the original and satisfy the same recursion.
The target is a largest or longest valid integer.

steps.detail: Store the complete digit string, used-digit set, and every legal deletion; do not store only a suffix.
For each deletion d, test m mod d=0 with integer arithmetic and require d to be certified valid.
Certify one-digit states first, then longer strings, recording a deletion witness for each accepted state.
Try deletions and digit placements at every position; descending order is only an ordering, not a maximality proof.
List the complete witness chain and exclude all longer or larger unused-digit states.

example.problem: Under a modified digit alphabet, call a distinct-digit integer recursively valid if deleting one digit yields a proper divisor that is recursively valid. Find the largest valid integer.
example.solution: Enumerate complete digit strings, allow every deletion position, certify predecessors by exact division, retain witnesses, and prove all larger states fail.

name: Single-Choice versus Multiple-Choice Truth-Table Verification
description: Handles conceptual option questions in which several statements may simultaneously be true. Distinguish a theorem characterization from a definition, evaluate every option independently, and make the final option string exactly match the proven truth set.
applicability: The prompt asks which statements or descriptions are correct.
Options may include both a definition and an equivalent theorem.
The question may be single-select or multi-select, and a correct analysis can still lose options during extraction.

steps.detail: Look for wording such as choose one, best, which are correct, or all that apply; if unclear, do not assume only one option.
For each option, state true or false and give a theorem, definition, or counterexample.
A definition and an equivalent characterization can both be correct; do not reject one merely because it is definitional.
Collect every option marked true and compare that set with the final answer before output.
Single choice uses one letter; multiple choice uses the complete ordered letter string without omissions or invented options.

example.problem: Which of several statements about compact subsets of a finite-dimensional metric space are correct, where one option gives a covering definition and another gives an equivalent closed-and-bounded criterion?
example.solution: Determine whether multiple selection is allowed, test every statement independently, recognize equivalent formulations, and output exactly the complete true-option set.

name: Five-Real Product Pairing via Quotient Distance
description: For five distinct positive reals, rewrites |ef-gh|<=Tfh as |e/h-g/f|<=T and uses crossing pairings of sorted adjacent ratios to obtain the sharp constant 1/2.
applicability: Five distinct positive real numbers
Choose four and relabel them in a product inequality
A best universal constant is required

steps.detail: Divide by fh, write quotients as products of r_i=u_i/u_{i+1}, apply the crossing-pairing lemma to logarithmic gaps, and use a limiting geometric progression for sharpness.

name: Bounded Integer Subset Sum Critical Window 1810
description: For nonnegative integer terms at most 100 and total at least 1810, obtains the sharp guaranteed subset-sum error 48 by the maximal attainable-sum gap argument and a critical residue construction.
applicability: Every term lies in [0,100]
The total crosses a prescribed target
The minimum worst-case approximation error is requested
Find the minimal d such that some subset I has |sum_{i in I} x_i-1810|<=d
The input is a sequence of integers x_1,...,x_n, each between 0 and 100
The total sum is at least 1810

steps.detail: Take maximal s<=1810; a local attainable-sum gap >=97 contradicts adding or deleting a term. The remaining critical window has radius 48, and the residue construction proves sharpness.

name: Strict Open-Interval Quadratic Constraint with 21 Variables
description: Finds the minimum number of values in (-1,1) satisfying sum x_i^2+(sum x_i)^2=20 and |sum x_i|<1, carefully excluding the tempting n=20 endpoint case.
applicability: Variables are constrained by a strict interval
A sum-of-squares expression is fixed
A minimum number of variables is sought
Find the smallest n for real x_1,...,x_n in the open interval (-1,1)
The exact constraint is sum_i x_i^2+(sum_i x_i)^2=20
The total sum has strict bound |x_1+...+x_n|<1

steps.detail: For fixed s, convexity gives sup sum x_i^2=20-2|s| in (-1,1)^20, contradicting 20-s^2. For n=21 use ten a, ten -a, and t with a=sqrt(1-t^2/10).

name: Truncated Cyclic Cubic Equality-Case Source Validation
description: Flags that the displayed pair x^2+y^2+z^2=3 and xy^3+yz^3+zx^3=3 cannot generically have eight isolated real solutions, so a missing condition must be restored before proof.
applicability: A source claims a finite equality-case count
Only two continuous equations in three real variables are displayed
The supplied answer conflicts with dimensional sanity checking
The displayed system asks for the number of real triples (x,y,z)
It contains exactly x^2+y^2+z^2=3 and xy^3+yz^3+zx^3=3
Check whether a finite-count claim is possible with only two equations in three real variables

steps.detail: Treat 8 only as the dataset reference answer; recover the original third condition rather than inventing a multiplier proof from an underdetermined statement.

name: Four-Digit-Residue DP up to 16 Digits
description: Counts natural numbers of at most 16 digits drawn from {0,1,2,8} and divisible by 3, including the official convention that counts zero.
applicability: Allowed decimal digits have residue multiplicities 1,1,2 modulo 3
A length bound is small and fixed
Leading-zero and zero conventions matter

steps.detail: Use A_{r,l+1}=A_{r,l}+A_{r-1,l}+2A_{r-2,l}, start nonzero-leading strings at (0,1,2), sum residue-zero counts through 16, then add zero to obtain 1431655765.

name: Triangular-Lattice Regular Hexagon Enumeration
description: Counts regular hexagons with lattice vertices inside a side-100 regular triangular-grid hexagon by summing legal translations of Eisenstein-lattice side vectors.
applicability: Vertices must lie in a triangular lattice
A large regular hexagonal boundary is given
Count all inscribed regular hexagons

steps.detail: Represent a side by p+q omega, rotate by omega and omega^2, count translations satisfying the three coordinate bounds, and divide six duplicate starting-side encodings. Ignore circles with no stated role.

name: Path Domino Minimax via Mod-7 Segment States
description: Analyzes alternating nonoverlapping domino placement on a 2020-cell path by the multiset of uncovered segment lengths, yielding 290 uncovered cells under optimal play.
applicability: A move covers two adjacent empty cells
Moves split intervals into residual segments
Players optimize the terminal number of uncovered cells

steps.detail: Induct on segment states modulo 7: Bob limits each complete block while Alice preserves the matching boundary state; combine 2020=288*7+4.

name: Domino and S-Tetromino Tiling Color-Imbalance 506
description: Minimizes dominoes in a 1008 by 1010 tiling by dominoes and rotatable S-tetrominoes using a periodic color imbalance and a boundary-strip construction.
applicability: A board is tiled by two polyomino types
One tile preserves a periodic coloring balance
A minimum number of the other tile is asked

steps.detail: S-tetrominoes contribute zero to the chosen imbalance while a domino repairs at most one unit, forcing 506; tile the interior periodically by S pieces and the boundary with exactly 506 dominoes.

name: Disjoint 3D Pillar Identification with 486 Queries
description: Determines the minimum color queries needed to reconstruct pairwise non-touching black 1x1x18 pillars in an 18-cube, with the promise of at least two pillars.
applicability: Objects are long axis-parallel pillars in a cube
Queries reveal individual cell states
All legal configurations must be distinguishable

steps.detail: An unqueried essential cross-section location leaves two legal pillar sets indistinguishable. Each of three directions needs 162 positions, and querying all 486 identifies every candidate pillar.

name: Opposite-Integer Avoidance Guarantee for 68 Pairs
description: Guarantees 43 hit pairs when erasing entries from 68 integer pairs while never erasing opposite integers, and uses a blocking construction for sharpness.
applicability: Each absolute value permits one of two signs
A pair scores when an endpoint is selected
Worst-case guaranteed score is required

steps.detail: Choose each sign randomly and fix it by conditional expectation; the prohibition on both (k,k) and (-k,-k) yields 43. Ignore undefined invisible-whiteboard prose.

name: Critical n-Line Cover Bound Binomial n Plus 2 Choose 2
description: Applies the critical line-cover lemma to a point set not coverable by n lines but coverable after every point deletion, giving binomial(n+2,2).
applicability: Deleting any point lowers the line-cover number
A maximum point count is sought
Noncyclicity excludes degeneration
A point set S is not coverable by n lines, but S-{X} is coverable by n lines for every X in S
The problem asks for maximum |S| with n=2012
It additionally excludes one circle passing through every point

steps.detail: The upper bound is |S|<=C(n+2,2), attained by the dual/projection construction. For n=2012, compute C(2014,2)=2027091.

name: 52-by-52 Square Overlay Equal-Coverage Bound
tags: number of tiles covering a cell
description: Maximizes cells having the same positive coverage under 52x52 square overlays on a 2011x2011 board, using residue-class row and column sums.
applicability: Fixed square windows overlap on a large grid
A maximum multiplicity class is requested
Board length has a nonzero remainder modulo window size
A finite collection of 52x52 square tiles is placed on a 2011x2011 board
Each cell records its coverage multiplicity
Maximize the number k of cells with one identical positive coverage value

steps.detail: With 2011=52*39-17, residue classes have 39 versus 38 terms; two-direction counting forces (52^2-35^2)*39-17^2=57392 exceptions. A stepped placement attains coverage 1 elsewhere, giving 3986729.

name: Personal Nonadjacency Number-Selection Draw Threshold
description: Finds the largest n for which two players can select every number from 1 to n when each player may not select consecutive numbers within that player's own history.
applicability: Numbers are chosen without repetition
